passage_text: Researchers at the University of Example studied the impact of three distinct instructional interventions on high school students' mathematics achievement. The study involved 240 participants randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group receiving standard classroom instruction, and three experimental groups each exposed to a different instructional strategy—Intervention A (peer tutoring), Intervention B (technology‑enhanced learning), and Intervention C (flipped classroom). Baseline assessments were administered before the intervention and post‑intervention assessments after an eight‑week period. The table below summarizes the mean scores (out of 100) for each group at both time points. The researchers hypothesized that all experimental groups would outperform the control group, with the greatest gains expected in the technology‑enhanced group. Data analysis included paired‑sample t‑tests and analysis of variance to evaluate within‑group changes and between‑group differences. The findings revealed statistically significant improvements for all experimental groups relative to control, with Intervention B showing the largest mean increase. These results suggest that incorporating technology into mathematics instruction may yield substantial benefits for student learning outcomes.
table_data:
Group | Baseline Score | Post-Intervention Score
Control | 68.5 | 70.2
Intervention A | 69.0 | 75.3
Intervention B | 68.8 | 80.1
Intervention C | 69.2 | 74.5
stem: What was the average improvement (post - baseline) for Intervention A?
explanation: The mean improvement for Intervention A is calculated as 75.3 – 69.0 = 6.3 points.
trap: Subtracting from the wrong baseline or mis-subtracting 75.3 - 69.0, which gives distractors such as 5.8 or 7.0.

stem: Which experimental design best addresses potential confounding variables in this study?

options.B: Randomized controlled trial with random assignment

explanation: Randomized controlled trials with random assignment distribute known and unknown confounders evenly across groups, enhancing internal validity.
trap: Choosing a quasi-experimental matched design because it sounds rigorous, although matching cannot balance unmeasured confounders the way random assignment does.

stem: Calculate the percent improvement for Intervention B.
trap: Dividing the 11.3-point gain by the post-intervention score (80.1) gives about 14.1%, close to option B; the baseline of 68.8 must be the denominator.

stem: Which statement is false regarding random assignment in this study?

options.A: It balances known and unknown confounders across groups on average
options.B: It eliminates the need for statistical control of confounders
options.C: It can be implemented using a random number generator

explanation: Correct: Random assignment balances confounders only on average, so chance imbalances can remain and statistical analysis is still needed. Why the others are wrong: A) balancing confounders on average is exactly what randomization does. C) a random number generator is a standard way to randomize. D) randomization strengthens internal validity.
trap: Believing randomization removes every need for statistical analysis or guarantees perfectly balanced groups in each sample.

stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?

options.A: Intervention B had the largest mean score gain (11.3 points) of the four groups.
options.B: Peer tutoring had no effect on scores.
options.D: No group improved more than the control group.

explanation: Correct: Gains were 1.7 (control), 6.3 (A), 11.3 (B) and 5.3 (C) points, so B gained the most. Why the others are wrong: B) Intervention A gained 6.3 points versus 1.7 for control. C) Intervention C rose from 69.2 to 74.5, an increase. D) all three interventions gained more than the control group.
trap: Jumping to a policy recommendation or to claims of no effect that the group means over eight weeks do not support.
